In addition to their action on monoamine receptors, various
imidazoline and guanidinium compounds also interact with a
physically distinet membrane protein termed the imidazoline/
ium-receptive site (IGRS)! (1-4). The site is usually
identified by using the benzodioxane-imidezoline anslog ["H]
idazoxan (2-8) and may be similar to the binding sites termed
imidazoline or non-adrenergic imidazoline-preferring binding
sites. IGRS is defined by its ligand recognition properties,
particularly its high affinity for imidezolines, such as ciraza
line and idazoxan, and for compounds with a guanidinium
‘moiety, such as guanabenz and amiloride. An apparently
related receptor (imidazole binding site) was initially ident-
fied by Emsberger et al (9) in radioligand binding studies
with the imidazoline [*H]p-aminoclonidine. This ste exhibits

IGRS jis found in tissue homogenates enriched in plasma-

the mitochondria in certain tissues (4). The molecules recog-
nized by IGRS elicit many effects (10, 11) including altered
fon flux (12-15), stimulation of insulin secretion (16), and
regulation of blood pressure vie sites in the central nervous
system (17-19), Some of these responses are mimicked by an
endogenous bioactive material, clonidine-displacing substance
(20-23), which is also recognized by IGRS (1, 8). However,
the endogenous substance is only partially purified, its struc-
ture is unknown, and its precise ole in eliciting various cell
responses is unclear. Although the synthetic ligands that are
recognized by IGRS and the imidazole binding site elicit
several cell responses, the signaling pathway involved and the
relative importance of IGRS in these events are controversial
